vignette:
Mele is a 31-year-old married dancer who grew up in an Oceanian family in the United States, and when she speaks about why she has come to treatment now, she returns to one repeated scene from childhood: nights in the family home when violence would erupt between the adults and she would be close enough to hear it, see enough of it, and understand that someone she depended on was not going to keep her safe. She remembers being very still, acutely aware of being in the room or just outside it, afraid that any movement or sound from her might draw attention. Certain names from that period remain painfully charged for her. If she hears one of those names said aloud now, even in an unrelated context, it can feel as if the room changes temperature around her and the old scene is suddenly there again. What makes these moments so disorienting is how quickly they arrive. She can be in the studio listening to corrections, or backstage while someone calls out for a cast member, and without warning she is no longer anchored in the present but caught in the full force of the childhood memory.

In the years after the violence, Mele developed a private way of carrying it that few people noticed. Sometimes when she recalled what happened, the strongest feeling was shame. She did not speak about the violence as something done by others so much as something that exposed something terrible about her. She had come to believe there was something about her that made the event happen, as if her very presence in the family had invited it or failed to stop it. Alongside that was a quieter but equally fixed sense of betrayal. The people she trusted most had not been what she needed them to be, and she became certain that people are not what they seem. Even when someone appeared warm or protective, part of her waited for the hidden version to emerge.

Her memory of the violence does not come in one consistent form. At times it returns with humiliating clarity and she is flooded with shame, wanting to hide her face, unable to bear what it means about her. At other times she can describe pieces of what happened in a flat, detached way, as if she is talking about a stranger’s childhood. In session she has noticed this shift herself: one moment her body tightens and her voice thins, and another moment she sounds almost puzzled by how little she feels. The numbness frightens her in its own way because it makes her feel cut off from herself, as though important parts of her experience happened to someone else.

Her work as a dancer places her in exactly the kinds of situations that can catch these reactions. She spends long hours in mirrored rehearsal spaces, under bright lights, with instructors, directors, and other dancers watching closely. Being observed is part of the job, but for Mele the sensation of being watched can turn sharply threatening. If she notices eyes on her from the edge of the room, or senses a director studying her without speaking, she becomes intensely self-conscious and braced. Her heart begins to pound, and that bodily feeling is itself another trigger. The instant she becomes aware of her own racing heart, it can pull her toward the old childhood terror so suddenly that she struggles to stay present in choreography. She has found herself stepping out to the hallway longer than necessary, lingering in dressing rooms, avoiding eye contact, or positioning herself at the back of the studio where she feels less exposed. Over months this has affected her work. She has missed chances to be featured because she appears hesitant during auditions, and at home her husband has grown confused by how often she says she is “fine” while remaining distant and hard to reach.

Mele has not told many people the full story because distrust comes easily to her. She listens for inconsistencies, assumes that kindness may conceal something else, and often feels she must manage everything alone. What finally brought her to seek help was a recent rehearsal in which a name was called out that echoed one tied to the violence at home. She felt instantly transported, then became aware of her heart hammering and of everyone in the room looking in her direction. She finished the rehearsal feeling numb and humiliated, then went home ashamed that she could not simply act like everyone else. She is seeking help now because she is tired of being overtaken without warning and tired of living as though other people cannot be trusted. What frightens her most is the possibility that this will keep happening in the studio, in her marriage, and anywhere she is seen; what she hopes for, cautiously, is to feel present in her own life without the past arriving in full around her.
